usage: The noodles are nice and chewy
면발 = the strands/body of the noodle; the #1 compliment for noodles
식감 (食感) = mouthfeel; this exact phrase is everywhere in food reviews
the doubled mimetic form intensifies it — even bouncier
-게 + cooking verb = cook it so it turns out chewy
examples: 떡이 참 쫄깃하네요.
The rice cake is really chewy.
simple praise; -네요 adds a warm 'oh, nice' reaction
갓 뽑은 면이라 쫄깃쫄깃해요.
It's freshly pulled noodles, so it's super chewy.
갓 + V-(으)ㄴ = freshly done; pairs naturally with the doubled form
사장님, 여기 문어가 안 질기고 쫄깃해서 또 왔어요.
Boss, the octopus here isn't tough but pleasantly chewy, so I came back.
real restaurant scene; 쫄깃하다 = good chewy vs 질기다 = bad tough, side by side
nuance: 쫄깃하다 is the GOOD chewy — the bouncy, springy, slightly elastic bite of fresh noodles, 떡 (rice cake), or well-cooked octopus, the kind that resists your teeth just enough and snaps back. The sharp dividing line every learner needs: 쫄깃하다 is praise, while its near-opposite 질기다 is the bad 'tough/rubbery' chewy you can't bite through; an overcooked steak is 질겨요, never 쫄깃해요. It is a 의태어-flavored native (non-Sino) word, so it carries a vivid, sensory, casual feel and is used freely in everyday speech and reviews — saying 면이 쫄깃해요 to a restaurant owner is a genuine compliment about 식감 (texture). It collocates above all with 면, 면발, 떡, 식감, and the cooking adverb 쫄깃하게. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: do not translate 'chewy gum/tough jerky' with 쫄깃하다 (that drifts into 질기다), and never inflect it like a verb — it is an adjective, so the modifier is 쫄깃한 면, never 쫄깃하는 면.

mistakes: Using 쫄깃하다 for tough meat you can't bite through. That negative 'tough/rubbery' sense is a different word, 질기다 — 쫄깃하다 is only the pleasant springy kind, so say 고기가 질겨요 for the bad case.
Saying 쫄깃하는 면. 쫄깃하다 is an adjective, so the present modifier is 쫄깃한 (쫄깃한 면), and you never use the verb-style -는.
Forcing 쫄깃하다 onto crispy fried food. Crispy is 바삭하다; 쫄깃하다 is specifically the elastic, springy texture, so 쫄깃한 치킨 sounds wrong unless you mean a soft, gummy crust.

usage: the single most-used pairing; 바삭한 + fried food
famous abbreviation of 겉은 바삭, 속은 촉촉
doubled mimetic form, intensified and very common
-게 + 튀기다, the standard way to talk about frying
examples: 과자가 바삭해요.
The cracker is crispy.
simplest possible use; 과자 = snack/cracker
튀김이 갓 나와서 엄청 바삭해요.
The fritters just came out, so they're super crispy.
갓 나오다 = just came out; freshness is what makes it 바삭
여기 돈까스는 겉이 바삭하고 안은 부드러워서 단골 됐어요.
The cutlet here is crispy outside and soft inside, so I became a regular.
real-life 단골(regular) scene; 겉/안 contrast captures 겉바속촉
nuance: 바삭하다 is the LIGHT, airy crunch of fried chicken, 튀김, fresh toast, crackers, or seaweed — a crisp that shatters cleanly, which is exactly why it is the headline selling point of fried food in Korea and the root of the famous slang 겉바속촉 (crispy outside, moist inside). Keep two boundaries straight: its opposite is 눅눅하다 (gone soft/soggy), so once fries lose their crisp Koreans say 눅눅해졌어요, not 바삭해요; and it must not be confused with 딱딱하다 (hard/stiff/rock-hard) — 바삭하다 breaks with a light snap, while 딱딱하다 means uncomfortably hard. It is a native sound-symbolic word (the doubled 바삭바삭 mimics the crunch), so it feels vivid and casual and pours out in mukbang and reviews. Habitual partners: 치킨, 튀김, 김, the adverb 바삭하게, and the verb 튀기다. The English-speaker pitfall: 'crunchy' in English also covers hard nuts or raw carrots (that firm crunch leans 아삭하다 for crisp veg or 딱딱하다 for hard), and of course never write the verb-style 바삭하는 — it is 바삭한 / 바삭해요.

Applying 바삭하다 to the firm crunch of fresh vegetables. That snap is 아삭하다 (crisp like lettuce, apples, cucumber); 바삭하다 is reserved for dry, fried, baked crispness.

usage: appetizing sour, unlike the plain/neutral 시다
set phrase for 탕수육, 귤, gummies — extremely common
무치다 = toss with seasoning, as in 무침 dishes
-아/어지다 = became; vinegar is the prototypical source
examples: 이 귤 새콤해요.
This tangerine is tangy.
simplest form; fruit is the easiest 새콤하다 context
냉면 국물이 새콤해서 입맛이 도네요.
The cold-noodle broth is tangy, so it whets my appetite.
everyday; 입맛이 돌다 = appetite picks up, a set phrase
비빔국수는 새콤하게 비벼야 제맛이죠.
Spicy mixed noodles are best when mixed tangy, that's the real flavor.
real cooking opinion; -게 makes it adverbial 'tangily', 제맛 = the proper taste
nuance: 새콤하다 is the appetizing, refreshing, mouth-watering sour of vinegar, citrus, and 무침/냉면 dishes — the sour that makes you want another bite rather than pucker up. The synonym map is the whole point: plain 시다 is just neutral 'sour' (a lemon 시다 simply reports the fact), while 시큼하다 is a sharper, sometimes off or fermented sour that can signal spoilage; 새콤하다 sits in the pleasant middle and is the only one of the three you use as praise. It is a native sound-symbolic adjective with a small, bright vowel (the 'ㅐ/ㅗ' feel diminutive and cute), which is why it reads as charming and casual and lives in the fixed combo 새콤달콤하다 (sweet-and-sour), plastered across snacks and ads. Habitual partners: 맛, 냄새 is rare here, but 무침, 냉면, 귤/레몬, and 새콤하게 (무치다/비비다) are everywhere. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 새콤하다 to say milk has 'gone sour' — spoiled sour is 시큼하다 or 쉬다/상하다 — and never write 새콤하는; it is 새콤한 / 새콤해요.

english: pleasantly spicy, with a nice kick
usage: set phrase for 떡볶이, 닭갈비 — the flavor everyone loves
natural way to request a spice level
examples: 국물이 매콤해요.
The broth has a nice kick.
simple; 매콤하다 pairs constantly with 국물
떡볶이는 매콤달콤한 게 제맛이죠.
Tteokbokki tastes best sweet-and-spicy, that's the real flavor.
everyday opinion; 제맛 = the true/proper taste
안 맵게 말고 살짝 매콤하게 해 주세요.
Not no-spice, just a little bit spicy, please.
real ordering scene; 살짝 = slightly, distinguishes a mild kick from full 맵게
nuance: 매콤하다 is a pleasant, appetizing spiciness — a warm, enjoyable kick — and it is built from the plain adjective 맵다 (hot/spicy) plus the diminutive-softening pattern that turns blunt taste words into cozy ones (맵다 → 매콤하다, just as 짜다 → 짭짤하다, 시다 → 새콤하다). That derivation is the key contrast: 맵다 can mean painfully, eye-watering hot, whereas 매콤하다 frames the heat as positive and manageable, which is why it praises 떡볶이, 찌개, and 닭갈비 and lives in the combo 매콤달콤하다 (sweet-and-spicy). Because it is the gentle form, register matters when ordering: 매콤하게 해 주세요 asks for 'a nice kick,' while 맵게 해 주세요 risks getting it genuinely fiery. Habitual partners: 양념, 국물, 떡볶이, 닭갈비, and 매콤하게. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 매콤하다 for unbearable heat — if it's too hot to eat, you must switch back to the base word (매워서 못 먹겠어요), because *너무 매콤해서 못 먹겠어요 sounds contradictory — and as always it is an adjective, so 매콤한 / 매콤해요, never 매콤하는.

Writing 매콤하는. The adjective forms are 매콤한 / 매콤해요 — never the verb-style -는.
Assuming 매콤하다 and 맵다 are interchangeable. 맵다 is neutral-to-painful 'spicy/hot'; 매콤하다 specifically frames the heat as enjoyable and moderate, so use 매콤하다 only when the spice is a good thing.

usage: -게 + 끓이다 = simmer it so it comes out 얼큰
warm and spicy in the stomach
그 따뜻한 느낌 — great for cold days/hangovers
examples: 국물이 얼큰해요.
The broth is hot and hearty.
simplest use; 얼큰하다 almost always sits with 국물
추운 날엔 얼큰한 국물이 최고예요.
On cold days, a hot spicy broth is the best.
everyday; -엔 = -에는, the warming-comfort nuance
어제 많이 마셨는데, 얼큰한 짬뽕으로 해장할래요?
I drank a lot yesterday — shall we cure the hangover with hearty jjamppong?
real situation; 해장 = curing a hangover, 얼큰하다's natural home
nuance: 얼큰하다 describes the warming, full-bodied, satisfying spicy heat of red-broth soups — 김치찌개, 짬뽕, 매운탕, 해장국 — and crucially it carries a feeling of comfort and physical warmth (몸이 풀리는 느낌), not just raw heat. The synonym contrast: 매콤하다 frames a light pleasant kick on almost any food, but 얼큰하다 is reserved for hot liquid that warms you from the inside, so the two are not swappable (a 떡볶이 sauce is 매콤하다, a steaming hangover soup is 얼큰하다). It collocates almost exclusively with 국물 / 국 / 탕 / 찌개 and the adverb 얼큰하게 (끓이다), and it is the go-to word for 추운 날 (cold days) and 해장 (curing a hangover). One register note Koreans know: 얼큰하다 also slangily means pleasantly tipsy (술이 얼큰하게 올랐다), but the food sense is the everyday default. The English-speaker pitfall: don't attach it to dry or solid food — *얼큰한 치킨 sounds wrong because there's no broth — and don't confuse it with the totally unrelated 느끼하다 (greasy/cloying); 얼큰하다 is hot-and-hearty, 느끼하다 is oily-and-heavy.

Using 얼큰하다 for any spicy dish. For a light, enjoyable kick on non-soup food use 매콤하다; reserve 얼큰하다 for hot, hearty, comforting broth.

usage: savory enough to go with rice
밥반찬 = a side dish for rice
examples: 이 과자 짭짤해요.
This snack is nice and salty.
simplest use; salty snacks are the easy context
감자튀김은 좀 짭짤해야 맛있어요.
Fries taste best when they're a little salty.
everyday; 좀 = a little (softener), 짭짤하다 = just-right salty
국이 짜지 않고 딱 짭짤하게 잘됐네요.
The soup isn't over-salty, it came out perfectly savory.
real cooking scene; 짜다 = too salty vs 짭짤하다 = pleasantly salty, contrasted directly
nuance: 짭짤하다 is the pleasant, moreish, savory saltiness that makes you keep eating — soy-braised dishes (장조림), fries, dried squid, salty snacks — and it is the diminutive-softened, positive cousin of 짜다 (salty), formed by the same pattern that turns 맵다 → 매콤하다 and 시다 → 새콤하다. That pairing is the essential contrast: 짜다 normally means unpleasantly over-salted (a complaint), while 짭짤하다 means the salt level is just right and tasty (a compliment), so 국이 짜요 says 'too salty' but 국이 짭짤해요 says 'perfectly savory.' It collocates with 맛, 반찬, 간식, 장조림 and is the natural praise for anything you'd call a 밥도둑 (a dish so savory it makes you eat extra rice). A well-known casual bonus: 짭짤하다 also means a side income is 'tidy/decent' (부수입이 짭짤하다). The English-speaker pitfall: never use 짭짤하다 to complain that food is too salty — for that you must switch to 짜다 (짜요), because 짭짤하다 is inherently positive — and it is an adjective, so it's 짭짤한 반찬 / 짭짤해요, never 짭짤하는.

usage: 비린 is the modifier form of 비리다
비린내 = the fishy smell; used as much as the adjective
the standard complaint about not-fresh fish
하나도 안 + adj = the strongest 'not at all' praise
examples: 이 회 좀 비려요.
This sashimi is a bit fishy.
simple, polite complaint about freshness
레몬을 뿌리면 비린내가 줄어요.
Squeezing lemon reduces the fishy smell.
everyday cooking tip; 비린내 (noun) in action
여기 회는 신선해서 하나도 안 비려요. 한번 드셔 보세요.
The sashimi here is so fresh it's not fishy at all — give it a try.
real recommending scene; 안 비리다 is the highest praise for raw fish
nuance: 비리다 is almost always negative: the off, fishy taste or smell of seafood — or even of blood (피 비린내) — that isn't fresh, the odor that turns people off raw fish. The companion noun 비린내 (fishy smell) is used every bit as much as the adjective, and because freshness in Korean food culture is judged largely by the *absence* of this quality, 안 비려요 ('not fishy at all') is genuine high praise for 회/생선. The synonym boundary matters: 비리다 is specific to fishy/raw-seafood odor, so don't stretch it to cover general bad smells — spoiled-rotten is 상한 냄새/쉰내, and a strong unpleasant smell in general is 고약하다. Habitual partners: 맛, 냄새, 비린내(가 나다/난다), 생선, 회, and the cooking fixes 레몬/식초/생강 (which 비린내를 잡다/없애다). The English-speaker pitfall: 비리다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 비린 (비린 맛, 비린내), never the verb-style 비리는 맛; and remember it is overwhelmingly a complaint word — you rarely use it positively except in the negated form 안 비리다.

Because freshness in Korean food culture is judged largely by the *absence* of this quality, 안 비려요 ('not fishy at all') is genuine high praise for 회/생선. Habitual partners: 맛, 냄새, 비린내(가 나다/난다), 생선, 회, and the cooking fixes 레몬/식초/생강 (which 비린내를 잡다/없애다).

The companion noun 비린내 (fishy smell) is used every bit as much as the adjective. 비리다 is specific to fishy/raw-seafood odor, so don't stretch it to cover general bad smells — spoiled-rotten is 상한 냄새/쉰내, and a strong unpleasant smell in general is 고약하다.

usage: 떫은 is the modifier form of 떫다
the textbook reference example of 떫다
kind of astringent / a touch puckery
also the standard word for strong tannins
examples: 이 감 떫어요.
This persimmon is astringent.
simplest use; 감 is the prototypical 떫다 food
덜 우린 차는 좀 떫어요.
Under-steeped tea is a bit astringent.
everyday; 덜 = under-/not enough, a common cause of 떫은맛
이 와인은 떫은맛이 강해서 고기랑 잘 어울려요.
This wine's tannins are strong, so it pairs well with meat.
real tasting scene; 떫은맛 = tannic astringency, food pairing context
nuance: 떫다 is the dry, mouth-puckering astringency of unripe persimmons, over-steeped tea, persimmon peel, or tannic wine — the sensation that makes your tongue feel rough and tight (혀가 까끌까끌한 느낌). In Korean it is treated as its own taste category, distinct from the other basics, and 감 (persimmon) is the cultural reference point everyone reaches for. The contrast learners must lock in is 떫다 vs 쓰다 (bitter): coffee, 한약(herbal medicine), and 여주(bitter melon) are 쓰다, while an unripe persimmon or strong tea is 떫다 — they are completely different sensations, not degrees of the same thing. Its softer relative is 떨떠름하다, 'a touch astringent.' Conjugation is fully regular (no irregular stem): 떫어요, 떫은, 떫고, 떫지 않다. Habitual partners: 맛, 감, 차, 와인, and 떫은맛(이 강하다/난다). The English-speaker pitfall: English lumps 'bitter' and 'astringent' loosely, so beginners over-use 쓰다 — reserve 쓰다 for true bitterness and use 떫다 for the puckery, drying sensation — and as an adjective it never takes verb endings, so it's 떫은 감 / 떫어요, never 떫는 감 or 떫는다.

usage: 뒷맛 = aftertaste; 깔끔한 뒷맛 = finishes clean
examples: 국물이 깔끔해요.
The broth is clean-tasting.
simplest food use; the most common collocation
맥주가 목 넘김이 깔끔해요.
The beer goes down clean.
everyday; 목 넘김 = the way it goes down the throat, a set drink-review phrase
여기 국밥은 안 느끼하고 깔끔해서 자주 와요.
The gukbap here isn't greasy but clean-tasting, so I come often.
real regular-customer scene; 깔끔하다 directly contrasted with 느끼하다
nuance: 깔끔하다 has a literal sense of 'tidy/neat/well-organized' (방이 깔끔하다, 일 처리가 깔끔하다), but in food talk it is a heavyweight review word meaning a clean, crisp, non-greasy flavor that leaves no heavy or oily residue — the precise opposite of 느끼하다 (greasy/cloying). That opposition is the contrast to remember: a clear 국물, a light lager, or a soup that 깔끔하게 떨어진다 earns 깔끔하다, whereas fatty 삼겹살 or cream sauce is 느끼하다, so calling rich greasy food 깔끔하다 is self-contradictory. Note it is broader than 담백하다 (plain, mild, not-rich): 담백하다 emphasizes a gentle, un-strong flavor, while 깔끔하다 emphasizes a clean *finish*; they overlap but aren't identical. Habitual partners: 맛, 국물, 뒷맛, 목 넘김, and 깔끔하게 (떨어지다/끝나다). You'll hear 깔끔해요 constantly in mukbang and restaurant reviews. The English-speaker pitfall: don't assume 깔끔하다 only means 'clean/tidy' as in spotless — in a food context it is a specific flavor compliment about a non-greasy, crisp taste, so translate it as 'clean-tasting,' not literally 'clean.'

usage: appetizing sweet, softer than plain 달다
set phrase, extremely common in food talk and ads
also used for smells, not only taste
examples: 이 케이크 달콤해요.
This cake is sweet.
simplest use; desserts are the core 달콤하다 context
딸기가 새콤달콤해서 계속 먹게 돼요.
The strawberries are sweet-and-sour, so I keep eating them.
everyday; -게 되다 = end up doing, and the fixed combo 새콤달콤
이 와인은 너무 달지 않고 은은하게 달콤해서 좋아요.
This wine isn't too sweet, just subtly sweet, so I like it.
real tasting scene; 은은하게 = subtly, 달다 (can imply too-sweet) contrasted with 달콤하다
nuance: 달콤하다 is a pleasant, appealing sweetness — and it is the diminutive-softened, more romantic cousin of the plain adjective 달다 (sweet), built by the same pattern that gives 시다 → 새콤하다 and 짜다 → 짭짤하다. That derivation is exactly the contrast to teach: 달다 is neutral and can carry a 'too sweet / cloying' edge (너무 달아서 못 먹겠어요), while 달콤하다 frames the sweetness as just-right and pleasing, which is why it praises desserts, fruit, and even aromas and lives in the combos 새콤달콤하다 (sweet-sour) and 달콤짭짤하다 (sweet-salty, salted-caramel style). It also has a strong figurative life: 달콤한 휴식 (a blissful rest), 달콤한 말 (sweet/honeyed words), 달콤한 사랑. Habitual partners: 디저트, 향, 케이크, 초콜릿, and the doubled-up combos. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 달콤하다 for sickly, overpowering sweetness — for 'too sweet to eat' you must switch to the base word (너무 달아서 못 먹겠어요), because 달콤하다 is inherently positive — and it is an adjective, so it's 달콤한 / 달콤해요, never 달콤하는.

Using only 달콤하다 and never 달다. They differ in tone — 달다 is neutral/can mean too-sweet, 달콤하다 is appealing — so choose by whether the sweetness is a good thing.

usage: can hint that food has turned
examples: 김치가 시큼해요.
The kimchi is sharply sour.
simple; fermented foods are the core context
우유에서 시큼한 냄새가 나요. 상한 것 같아요.
The milk smells sour. I think it's gone bad.
everyday; 상하다 = to spoil, the warning-sign use
이 빵 시큼한 거 보니 사워도우인가 봐요.
This bread tastes sour, so it must be sourdough.
real situation; -나 보다 = must be, here the sour is intentional/positive
nuance: 시큼하다 is a sharper, more piercing sour than the appetizing 새콤하다 — context decides whether it's good or a warning. The three-way map is the whole lesson: plain 시다 is neutral 'sour'; 새콤하다 is the pleasant, mouth-watering tang you praise; and 시큼하다 is the strong, biting sour that can be desirable in well-fermented 묵은지 or sourdough but also flags food starting to spoil (sour milk, off rice). So the same word can be positive (묵은지라 시큼해요 = nicely aged) or a red flag (시큼한 냄새가 나요 = this might be off), and the listener reads it from context. It is a native sound-symbolic adjective; the heavier vowel (ㅣ/ㅡ) versus 새콤하다's bright vowel is itself part of why it feels sharper and edgier. Habitual partners: 냄새, 맛, 김치/묵은지, 우유, and 시큼하게/시큼한. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 시큼하다 for the gentle tang of citrus, dressing, or 무침 — that pleasant sour is 새콤하다 — and as an adjective it's 시큼한 / 시큼해요, never 시큼하는.

english: tough, chewy in a bad way (hard to chew)
usage: the single most common complaint use
negative; the opposite of 쫄깃한 식감
the standard praise for good meat
examples: 이 고기 질겨요.
This meat is tough.
simplest complaint form
오래 익혔더니 오히려 더 질겨졌어요.
I cooked it longer and it actually got tougher.
everyday; 오히려 = on the contrary, -아/어지다 = became
사장님, 죄송한데 이 고기가 너무 질겨서 못 먹겠어요.
Excuse me, sorry, but this meat is so tough I can't eat it.
real complaint-to-staff scene; polite framing softens a negative judgment
nuance: 질기다 is the BAD chewy: meat or seafood so tough and rubbery it's hard to bite through — and it is the exact negative counterpart of the praised 쫄깃하다 (pleasantly springy/elastic). Locking this pair down is the priority, because English 'chewy' maps onto both and learners constantly swap them: an overcooked steak or stringy squid is 질겨요, while fresh bouncy noodles or well-cooked octopus are 쫄깃해요 — same English word, opposite verdict. It collocates with 고기, 식감, 오징어/문어, and the contrast 질기지 않고 부드럽다 (not tough but tender). Note the conjugation is regular (있다/먹다-type, not an irregular stem): 질겨요, 질긴, 질기고, and it becomes 질겨지다 ('to get tougher'). Beyond food, 질기다 also describes something stubborn and persistent — 질긴 인연 (a tie that won't break), 목숨이 질기다 (hard to kill / tenacious). The English-speaker pitfall: never use 질기다 as praise the way 'chewy' can be positive in English — if you mean the good springy bite, you must switch to 쫄깃하다 — and it is an adjective, so it's 질긴 고기 / 질겨요, never 질기는.
